headline: Chip-specific selling and rising hike odds keep tone defensive
body: The last full session (Friday) left the tape with a narrower story than a simple risk-off label suggests. The Nasdaq fell about 2.1% and the S&P 500 about 1.1%, capping the Nasdaq's worst week since June at roughly -4.5%, while the Dow was essentially flat on the day and the only one of the three to end the week higher. The tell is in the dispersion: a semiconductor ETF benchmark dropped more than 4%, triple the S&P's decline, pointing to concentrated unwinding in AI-capex-linked names rather than a broad flight from equities. Megacaps outside that cluster held up fine, including a record high for one large-cap tech name the same day, reinforcing that this reads as a crowded-trade correction in a specific pocket of the market rather than an index-wide growth scare.

The macro backdrop adds an unusual twist: futures-implied odds of a Fed rate hike by December have risen sharply over the past month (one dataset put it near 74%, up from roughly 50%), a reversal from the cut-focused narrative that dominated earlier in the year, following a hotter September CPI print. That's landing alongside a jump in oil, with Brent pushing toward $110 on renewed Middle East supply risk, a combination that pressures growth-stock valuations from two directions at once (higher discount rates, higher input-cost inflation) rather than one. Retail-sentiment searches turned up little specific or current chatter today, so this read leans on index price action, options-implied rate odds, and the oil move rather than social-media positioning.
